title: Who was the first to "paint the town red"? | IDIOM ORIGINS

entries.note: The German word for the midwife who visits new parents several times after a birth.
A metaphorical word or phrase, from Latin [[from:idioma]], something used by an individual or small group, going back to Greek idios, private; related to [[same-root:idiot]].
From Greek idiotes, from idios, private; the first idiots were private, non-professional people, hence untrained and ignorant; shares its root with [[same-root:idiom]].
A superstitious way to wish performers luck by wishing them harm; theories about stage curtains or stomping audiences are untrue; widespread only from the early 1900s.
Jess's favourite foreign [[equivalent:break a leg]], answered with [[see:speriamo che non caghi]].
The reply to the Italian [[see:in culo alla balena]], wishing that the whale does not relieve itself.
From [[from:John Dennis]], whose thunder sound effect from his flop [[see:Appius and Virginia]] was reused in [[see:Macbeth]]; it now means stealing someone's idea.
Playwright and critic who invented a realistic thunder effect and complained that others would [[see:steal someone's thunder]].
John Dennis's 1709 play, a flop, for which he created the new thunder effect behind [[see:steal someone's thunder]].
Shakespeare's play, staged using John Dennis's thunder system, which prompted [[see:steal someone's thunder]].
From [[from:John Gay]]'s poem [[see:New Song on New Similes]], where he would be this cool if a lady returned his advances; cucumbers stay cooler than their surroundings.
Poet whose [[see:New Song on New Similes]] is the source of [[see:cool as a cucumber]].
John Gay's poem full of elaborate similes, including [[see:cool as a cucumber]] and [[see:drunk as a piper]].

entries.term: my passion is as mustard strong
entries.note: One of the elaborate similes in the poem that gave [[see:cool as a cucumber]].
Another simile from the poem that gave [[see:cool as a cucumber]].

Wrongly credited to the [[see:Marquess of Waterford]] in [[see:Melton Mowbray]]; an 1800s Americanism, likely from fire lighting up buildings, maybe echoing [[see?:Dante's Inferno]] via [[see:Oscar Wilde]].
English town famous for pork pies that claims to be the birthplace of [[see:paint the town red]].
Said to have daubed a toll booth and town with red paint after the races in 1837, a story emerging decades after his death.
Supposedly said [[see:paint the town red]] came from [[see:Dante's Inferno]]; often falsely quoted, he wrote about painting the old world red in [[see:The Canterville Ghost]].
Said to contain a line about those who painted the world scarlet with sins, though Rob couldn't find it in any translation.
Oscar Wilde's spooky story mentioning young fellows painting the old world red, possibly referring to Dante.
From hunting, where beaters struck bushes to flush birds out for others; recorded in a 15th-century poem; the sense of indirect provocation appears in the 1700s.
Lying mortally wounded on the ground; one of many variants such as [[equivalent:bite the grass]] and [[equivalent:bite the earth]], going back to early Middle English.
Earliest variant of [[equivalent:bite the dust]], from 12th-century early Middle English: many mouths bit the grass.
Variant of [[equivalent:bite the dust]], found in a 16th-century translation of the Aeneid as bitten the earth.
One of the variants of [[equivalent:bite the dust]].
One of the variants of [[equivalent:bite the dust]].
One of the variants of [[equivalent:bite the dust]].
From soldiers biting soft lead bullets to endure pain without anaesthesia; first recorded by Francis Grose about whippings with the [[see:cat o' nine tails]], later used by Kipling.
A whip; wrongly proposed as the origin of cat idioms like [[see:let the cat out of the bag]] and [[see:cat got your tongue]].

entries.term: let the cat out of the bag
entries.note: Linked to [[see:pig in a poke]]: revealing that the bagged pig you bought was actually an inferior cat.
Buying a pig in a bag that turns out on opening not to be what you expected, perhaps a cat.
Not from whipping with the cat o' nine tails; likely a cute thing said to children, cats chasing wiggly things, like [[see:got your nose]].
Playful phrase said to children, compared with [[see:cat got your tongue]].
Literally biting down on your tongue so you can't speak; it goes back a long way, much like [[see:bite your lip]].
Largely the same as [[see:bite your tongue]], though lip-biting also signals flirtation or hesitation; found as early as about 1380.
Not from bells for people buried alive but horse racing: a [[from:ringer]] was a swapped-in horse, and [[from:dead]] means spot-on.
Falsely linked to graveside bells for those buried alive; probably from boxing, where the end-of-round bell saves a fighter from being counted out.
In horse racing, a fraudulent horse entered in place of another, which gave [[gave:dead ringer]].
Meaning spot-on or exact, as in [[see:dead giveaway]] and [[gave:dead ringer]].
Example of [[see:dead]] meaning spot-on.
Really does involve bells rung at someone's death, unlike [[see:saved by the bell]].
A bell rung on someone's death, genuinely connected with the dead, unlike [[see:saved by the bell]].
Not from a condemned man's last pub drink before the gallows cart; an American idiom shortened from [[from:on the water wagon]].
American phrase from street-spraying water wagons that kept dust down; someone aboard would choose water over alcohol; it gave [[gave:on the wagon]].
Unclear whether ironic or sincere; a drunk squire uses it in Fielding's 1734 comedy, and an 1834 quote implies judges drank after dinner.
From wealthy, idle lords having time to get drunk; dating to at least the 17th century, it sounds dated to Jess beside [[see:drunk as a skunk]].
Appalachian expression Jess prefers over [[see:drunk as a lord]], mainly because it rhymes.
Probably from dead cats and dogs washed down streets in downpours, as in [[see:Jonathan Swift]]'s [[see:A Description of a City Shower]]; animals falling from thatch is unlikely.
Popular poet whose 1710 poem described dead animals swept along by floods, though he never wrote [[see:raining cats and dogs]].

entries.term: A Description of a City Shower
entries.note: Swift's 1710 poem describing dead cats and drowned puppies tumbling down a flood, linked to [[see:raining cats and dogs]].
A minced form of [[from:fuck the dog]], from military and aviator slang, meaning a blunder by the 1960s; popularised by Tom Wolfe's [[see:The Right Stuff]].
Military slang from at least the 1930s, first meaning to loaf around, later to blunder; the vulgar original of [[gave:screwed the pooch]].
Tom Wolfe's book on swaggering test pilots, which explained [[see:screwed the pooch]] and helped popularise it.
An American phrase Rob found in a dictionary; relatively old and unrelated to the sexual sense, connected to [[from:boner]] meaning a joke.
In the 1920s a joke, as in Jess's old joke book called Boners.

entries.term: not in a Month of Sundays
entries.note: Sundays dragged because of religious restrictions, so a month of them is very long; an 1849 letter links it to there being no Sunday post.
Either from the rare [[from:blue moon]], or older, from the idea that the moon is never blue, so it will never happen.
Two full moons in one calendar month, rare because a year has 12 calendar months but 13 lunar months.
Shortened from [[from:when pigs fly with their tails forward]]; [[see:Lewis Carroll]] is among the first recorded users of the short form.

entries.term: when pigs fly with their tails forward
entries.note: The original, more absurd form of [[gave:when pigs fly]], quoted from 1581 and once far more common.
Among the first recorded users of the short [[see:when pigs fly]], in the Duchess's retort to Alice in [[see:Alice's Adventures in Wonderland]].
Contains the Duchess's line about pigs having the right to fly, an early short [[see:when pigs fly]].

entries.term: by the skin of your teeth
entries.note: From the Book of Job's [[from:with the skin of my teeth]], meaning gums as one's last flesh; popularised by [[see:The Skin of Our Teeth]].

entries.term: with the skin of my teeth
entries.note: The Book of Job phrase in the King James and Geneva Bibles, referring to the gums, which gave [[gave:by the skin of your teeth]].
1940s Thornton Wilder comedy-drama of characters surviving danger by luck, which helped cement [[see:by the skin of your teeth]] as narrow escape.
From the [[from:Riot Act]]; to tell someone to stop or else, now often heard of football managers at half-time.
British law after the Jacobite rebellion requiring groups of 12 or more to disperse when it was read; repealed in England and Wales in 1967.
British football-pundit phrase for great disappointment, perhaps from [[from?:as melancholy as a sick parrot]] in [[see:Aphra Behn]]'s 1682 play The False Count.

entries.term: as melancholy as a sick parrot
entries.note: Line spoken in Aphra Behn's 1682 play The False Count, the supposed source of [[gave?:sick as a parrot]].
Playwright of The False Count, where a character says [[see:as melancholy as a sick parrot]].
Dogs lived outdoors in poor conditions and often carried mange or plague; dating to the early 1700s.
Promising something absurd if a claim were true; earlier [[from:I'll eat Old Rowley's hat]]; Dickens's Pickwick Papers probably popularised an emphatic usage.
Earlier version of [[gave:I'd eat my hat]], referring to [[see:Old Rowley]], King Charles II.
Nickname of King Charles II, reportedly from a prolific stallion, matching his many mistresses and illegitimate children; unverified.
Being so angry you dislodge or throw down your wig; relatively recent, probably 1940s, like [[see:flip out]]; related to [[see:flip your lid]].
Discussed in a previous Words Unravelled episode.
An exclamation, one of several wig idioms related to [[see:flip your wig]].
An idiom for a public fight or rumble on the green, where wigs get knocked off.
Like [[see:flip your wig]], probably from the 1940s or later.
Related to [[see:flip your wig]], since lid is also a word for hat.

entries.term: pull the wool over someone's eyes
entries.note: Wool here meant a wig pulled over someone's face to obscure their view, nothing to do with sheep.
